new_statements.quote: CSB data highlight that the stress pattern system in this language variety is almost totally systematic; it is a language variety with iambic feet. Further, CSB data show up that stress is culminative at phonological level. It is also rhythmically distributed. The absence of stress assimilation is supported by CSB data as well. Since the location of stress is predictable, its stress pattern is fixed. The data, likewise, confirm that stress system in CSB is a mixture of morphological and rhythmic. Meanwhile, stress pattern in complex words indicate the suffixes attract the primary stress. Besides, in negative and prohibitive forms, prefixes m{- and n{- get the primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Central Sarawani Balochi (Iran) has predictable, fixed stress built on iambic (right-headed) feet; in suffixed words the suffixes attract primary stress, i.e. primary stress sits at the right edge of the word; secondary stress is distributed rhythmically. Reading is from the abstract only, so 'fixed: final syllable' is a low-confidence gloss of 'iambic feet + suffixes attract primary stress'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Abstract: stress 'is also rhythmically distributed' and the article treats 'the position of primary and secondary stress in mono-morphemic words, verbal paradigms, compound words, complex words, pair words'; no rule readable.
new_statements.exceptions: Negative and prohibitive prefixes ma-/na- take primary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Barker & Mengal 1969 describe Rakhshani Baluchi as spoken by co-author Aqil Khan Mengal and studied in Quetta, Pakistan (preface P.100; Makrani and Eastern Mari-Bugti material was collected but the course is Rakhshani). The 'Soohani 2010 MA thesis' open record is actually the DOAJ record of Soohani, Ahangar & van Oostendorp 2012, 'Stress Pattern System in Central Sarawani Balochi' (IJALS 3(1): 151-194), on the Sarawan variety of Sistan and Baluchestan, Iran. Both are Western Balochi varieties under west2368; the catalog's fixed: final syllable record most likely reflects Sarhaddi/standard descriptions (Jahani & Korn 2009 per Soohani 2017).

new_statements.quote: The highest pitch-stress (the 3) cannot occur on the last syllable of the utterance (unless the utterance consists of only one syllable). If the word or sequence before the last syllable is of the pattern CV(V̄)CVCC or CV(V̄)CV̄C (V=/y, w, ə/; V̄=/i, e, u, o, a/), then pitch-stress 3 falls on the second V or V̄: CV²CVCC³ or CV²CV̄C³. If the sequence before the utterance-final syllable is a monosyllabic word (#CVC, #CV̄C, #VC, #VCC, #V̄C, #CV̄, etc.), then pitch-stress 3 falls upon it. If the sequence before the utterance-final syllable is CVCVC, then the 3 falls upon the first V: CV³CVC² (or 1). [p. 2, sec. 1.104] ... The prefix /nə/ is used to negate an indicative verb. Since this prefix always bears the main word stress, the rules given for stress in Sec. 1.104 do not apply [p. 131, sec. 7.201]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records fixed final stress. Barker & Mengal describe a weight-sensitive rule for Rakhshani: final stress only when the final syllable is heavy (long vowel or CC coda); a light final syllable in a disyllable yields initial stress (kə́ləm 'pen', CVCVC -> 'the 3 falls upon the first V'). So the type differs (weight-sensitive vs fixed final), though the two agree for words with heavy final syllables (rəzā́n, kwčə́kk), and the negative prefix nə- taking main stress matches the prefix exception in Soohani et al. and Jahani. Caveat: the description is framed as an 'intonation pattern' and 'pitch-stress' of the utterance, not as a word-stress section; but the authors elsewh…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rakhshani Baluchi word prominence ('pitch-stress', the high tone 3 of the 2-3-1 declarative contour) is predictable from syllable weight: in a disyllable the second (final) syllable takes it if it is heavy - long vowel (/i e u o a/) or closed by two consonants - as in rəzā́n 'vessel' (CVCV̄C) and kwčə́kk 'dog' (CVCVCC); if both syllables are light (CVCVC with short vowels /y w ə/ and a single final consonant) the first syllable takes it, as in kə́ləm 'pen'; monosyllables carry it. The utterance-final syllable (in the examples the enclitic copula /e/) cannot carry the high pitch-stress. Ordinary word stress is left unmarked because it is predictable; only emphatic stress and the unpredictable stress on certain verbal prefixes are marked (p. xxvii: 'Stresses are marked by /ˊ/ (emphatic stress), and /ˋ/ (nonpredictable stress falling upon certain verbal prefixes)'; p. lviii: 'Two stresses: (a) /ˊ/, emphatic stress, which may fall upon an emphasised word in the utterance; and (b) /ˋ/, a special word stress which occurs with certain verbal prefixes.').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary-stress rule. In coordinative compounds of the type /barr-w-bedy/ 'each substantive constituent retains its own word stress. The stress on the first element is weaker, however' (p. 170, sec. 8.200); likewise /ma[h]ari-svar/ 'camel-rider': 'both /ma[h]ari/ and /svar/ have separate word stresses, although that of the former is weaker' (p. 181, sec. 9.102).
new_statements.exceptions: The negative prefix /nə/ 'always bears the main word stress', overriding the sec. 1.104 rule; such 'unpredictable (or "irregular") word stress' is marked /ˋ/ (p. 131, sec. 7.201). Emphatic stress may fall on any emphasised word; extra-high pitch-stress marks contrastive emphasis (sec. 3.902 ff.). The placement rule is stated only for monosyllables and disyllables before the utterance-final syllable; longer words are not covered.
new_statements.identity_note: Barker & Mengal 1969 describe Rakhshani Baluchi as spoken by co-author Aqil Khan Mengal and studied in Quetta, Pakistan (preface P.100; Makrani and Eastern Mari-Bugti material was collected but the course is Rakhshani). The 'Soohani 2010 MA thesis' open record is actually the DOAJ record of Soohani, Ahangar & van Oostendorp 2012, 'Stress Pattern System in Central Sarawani Balochi' (IJALS 3(1): 151-194), on the Sarawan variety of Sistan and Baluchestan, Iran. Both are Western Balochi varieties under west2368; the catalog's fixed: final syllable record most likely reflects Sarhaddi/standard descriptions (Jahani & Korn 2009 per Soohani 2017).

readall_conflicts: The catalog's fixed: final syllable entry (StressTyp2) disagrees with the one primary description read in full here: Barker & Mengal 1969 (Rakhshani, Quetta) give a weight-sensitive rule in which a heavy final syllable (long vowel or CC coda) attracts the high pitch-stress but a light final syllable in a disyllable loses it to the first syllable (kə́ləm 'pen' vs rəzā́n 'vessel', kwčə́kk 'dog'); the two agree only for heavy-final words. The Soohani et al. 2012 abstract (Central Sarawani, Iran; full text not obtained) says stress is fixed and predictable with iambic feet and suffix-attracted primary stress, which is compatible with the catalog's final stress but does not settle weight sensitivity; Soohani's later 2017 thesis on the same Iranian dialects (already held by the project, sec. 3.3, pp. 81 ff.) reports the final syllable attracts primary stress but heavy penults can take it, and cites Jahani & Korn 2009 for final stress in Western (Sarhaddi) Balochi versus weight-based stress in Southern dialects. So within the west2368 umbrella the sources split by dialect: Rakhshani (Barker & Mengal) weight-sensitive; Sarhaddi (Jahani & Korn, as reported) final; Sarawani (Soohani) right-edge iambic with weight effects. All sources agree that the negative/prohibitive prefix na-/ma- takes primary stress.

sources.quote: 'Stress normally falls on the last syllable of the word for nouns and adjectives. Some pronouns, adverbs, adpositions, conjunctions and interjections take their stress on the first syllable. ... All clitics ... are unstressed. Stress also varies in different dialects, and divergences from the normal stress patterns are not uncommon. (It may, in fact, be more appropriate to call this feature tone than to call it stress.)' Indirect for west2368: the standard described is built on Southern Balochi dialects (p. 20), not Western; consistent with final-stress-as-norm but not evidence for the Western
